title: A Multi-Stranded Math Curriculum
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane describes restructuring his 7th-grade maths curriculum away from six sequential single-topic units and toward three parallel strands: four topics taught roughly in sequence, plus rational numbers and expressions/equations stretched across the entire year as continuous strands. He argues the sequential-unit model forces him to push through material before students have consolidated it, since falling behind schedule isn't an option, and that this especially damages the two hardest, most foundational topics. By running rational numbers and expressions/equations in parallel with everything else -- a few minutes of practice most days rather than one concentrated block -- he creates the space for spaced, interleaved practice, easier review of prerequisite skills, and finer-grained breakdown of skills into smaller steps. He credits the underlying idea to the Direct Instruction tradition's use of parallel strands, contrasting it with what he sees as a wave of newer US curricula that emphasise big ideas and rigor without enough built-in review.
points: Kane's core structural diagnosis is that sequential single-topic units create an unavoidable trade-off: move on to stay on schedule, or fall behind to consolidate -- and the multi-stranded approach is designed to remove that trade-off entirely for the hardest topics.

His worked example (2x+1=11 building step by step to two-step equations with negative fractions and decimals) shows the practical payoff of stretching a strand across the year: harder variations get introduced only once easier ones are secure, without needing an entire dedicated unit.

The English-curriculum comparison is his sharpest argument for the model: no English teacher would confine vocabulary work to one unit and never touch it again, yet math curricula routinely do exactly that with foundational skills.

Kane credits the underlying idea to the book Direct Instruction: A Practitioner's Handbook, explicitly inviting readers skeptical of Direct Instruction to engage with the source rather than dismiss the idea by association.
quotes: I’ve always felt like the math curriculum moves too fast. I teach topic A, and I know students could use some more practice to consolidate their understanding. But we have to move on to topic B.
Math is sequential. New topics build on earlier ones. But math also isn’t one giant staircase.
Four of the six units are sequenced a bit like before, though now there’s more time for each unit. The other two units stretch in parallel through the entire year.
An English teacher would never create artificial divisions where unit one focuses only on vocabulary, and then doesn't do any work on vocabulary the rest of the year.
This approach to curriculum does not work if you are set on having a single objective for each lesson.
I learned about this idea from the book Direct Instruction: A Practitioner’s Handbook.
